AGENCY:
Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, Department of Commerce.
SUMMARY:
As a result of the determinations by the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) and the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that revocation of the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on standard steel welded wire mesh from Mexico would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and countervailable subsidies, and material injury to an industry in the United States, Commerce is publishing a notice of continuation of these AD and CVD orders.
DATES:
Applicable September 23, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Kayden Jenson, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-0967.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On April 12 and August 9, 2021, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD and CVD orders on standard steel welded wire mesh from Mexico.[1]
On March 2, 2026, the ITC instituted,[2]
and Commerce initiated,[3]
the first sunset review of the
Orders,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act). As a result of its reviews, Commerce determined that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and/or countervailable subsidies, and therefore, notified the ITC of the magnitude of the margins of dumping and subsidy rates likely to prevail should the
Orders
be revoked.[4]
On September 21, 2026, the ITC published its determination, pursuant to sections 751(c) and 752(a) of the Act, that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury to an industry in the United States within a reasonably foreseeable time.[5]
Scope of the Orders
The merchandise covered by the scope of the orders is standard steel welded wire mesh from Mexico. For a full description of the scope of the
Orders, see
the appendix to this notice.
Continuation of the Orders
As a result of the determinations by Commerce and the ITC that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of dumping, countervailable subsidies, and material injury to an industry in the United States, pursuant to section 751(d)(2) of the Act, Commerce hereby orders the continuation of the
Orders.
U.S. Customs and Border Protection will continue to collect AD and CVD cash deposits at the rates in effect at the time of entry for all imports of subject merchandise.
The effective date of the continuation of the
Orders
will be September 23, 2026.[6]
Pursuant to section 751(c)(2) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(c)(2), Commerce intends to initiate the next five-year reviews of the
Orders
not later than 30 days prior to fifth anniversary of the date of the last determination by the ITC.
Administrative Protective Order (APO)
This notice also serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305(a)(3), which continues to govern business proprietary information in this segment of the proceeding. Timely written notification of the return or destruction of APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective order, is hereby requested. Failure to comply with the regulations and terms of an APO is a violation which is subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
These five-year (sunset) reviews and this notice are in accordance with sections 751(c) and 751(d)(2) of the Act, and published in accordance with section 777(i) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.218(f)(4).
Dated: October 19, 2026.
Scot Fullerton,
Acting Deputy Assistant Secretary for Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Operations.
Appendix
Scope of the Orders
The merchandise covered by this order is uncoated standard welded steel reinforcement wire mesh (wire mesh) produced from smooth or deformed wire. Subject wire mesh is produced in square and rectangular grids of uniformly spaced steel wires that are welded at all intersections.
( printed page 67275)
Sizes are specified by combining the spacing of the wires in inches or millimeters and the wire cross-sectional area in hundredths of square inch or millimeters squared. Subject wire mesh may be packaged and sold in rolls or in sheets.
Subject wire mesh is currently produced to ASTM specification A1064/A1064M, which covers carbon-steel wire and welded wire reinforcement, smooth and deformed, for concrete in the following seven styles:
1. 6X6 W1.4/W1.4 or D1.4/D1.4
2. 6X6 W2.1/W2.1 or D2.1/D2.1
3. 6X6 W2.9/W2.9 or D2.9/D2.9
4. 6X6 W4/W4 or D4/D4
5. 6X12 W4/W4 or D4/D4
6. 4X4 W2.9/W2.9 or D2.9/D2.9
7. 4X4 W4/W4 or D4/D4
The first number in the style denotes the nominal spacing between the longitudinal wires and the second number denotes the nominal spacing between the transverse wires. In the first style listed above, for example, “6X6” denotes a grid size of six inches by six inches. “W” denotes the use of smooth wire, and “D” denotes the use of deformed wire in making the mesh. The number following the W or D denotes the nominal cross-sectional area of the transverse and longitudinal wires in hundredths of a square inch (
i.e.,
W1.4 or D1.4 is .014 square inches).
Smooth wire is wire that has a uniform cross-sectional diameter throughout the length of the wire.
Deformed wire is wire with indentations or raised transverse ribs, which results in wire that does not have a uniform cross-sectional diameter throughout the length of the wire.

SUMMARY:
As a result of the determinations by the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) and the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) that revocation of the antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) orders on certain small vertical shaft engines between 99cc and 225cc, and parts thereof (small vertical engines) from the People's Republic of China (China) would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping, countervailable subsidies, and material injury to an industry in the United States, Commerce is publishing a notice of continuation of these AD and CVD orders.
DATES:
Applicable October 26, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Zachary Shaykin (AD) or Bushra Bani-Salman (CVD), AD/CVD Operations, Offices II and IX, respectively, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-2638 or (202) 482-9170, respectively.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On May 4, 2021, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the
Orders
on small vertical engines from China.[1]
On April 1, 2026, Commerce initiated the first sunset review of the
Orders,
pursuant to section 751(c) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).[2]
As a result of its reviews, Commerce determined that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to the continuation or recurrence of dumping and countervailable subsidies, and therefore, notified the ITC of the magnitude of the margin of dumping and subsidy rates likely to prevail should the
Orders
be revoked.[3]
On October 20, 2026, the ITC published its determination, pursuant to sections 751(c) and 752(a) of the Act, that revocation of the
Orders
would likely lead to continuation or recurrence of material injury to an industry in the United States within a reasonably foreseeable time.[4]
Scope of the Orders
The scope of the
Orders
consists of spark-ignited, non-road, vertical shaft engines, whether finished or unfinished, whether assembled or unassembled, whether mounted or unmounted, primarily for walk-behind lawn mowers. Engines meeting this physical description may also be for other non-hand-held outdoor power equipment, including but not limited to, pressure washers. The subject engines are spark ignition, single-cylinder, air cooled, internal combustion engines with vertical power take off shafts with a minimum displacement of 99 cubic centimeters (cc) and a maximum displacement of up to, but not including, 225cc. Typically, engines with displacements of this size generate gross power of between 1.95 kilowatts (kw) to 4.75 kw.
Engines covered by this scope normally must comply with and be certified under Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) air pollution controls title 40, chapter I, subchapter U, part 1054 of the Code of Federal Regulations standards for small non-road spark-ignition engines and equipment. Engines that otherwise meet the physical description of the scope but are not certified under 40 CFR part 1054 and are not certified under other parts of subchapter U of the EPA air pollution controls are not excluded from the scope of these proceedings. Engines that may be certified under both 40 CFR part 1054 as well as other parts of subchapter U remain subject to the scope of these proceedings.
Certain small vertical shaft engines, whether or not mounted on non-hand-held outdoor power equipment, including but not limited to walk-behind lawn mowers and pressure washers, are included in the scope. However, if a subject engine is imported mounted on such equipment, only the engine is covered by the scope. Subject merchandise includes certain small vertical shaft engines produced in the subject country whether mounted on outdoor power equipment in the subject country or in a third country. Subject engines are covered whether or not they are accompanied by other parts.
For purposes of these
Orders,
an unfinished engine covers at a minimum a sub-assembly comprised of, but not limited to, the following components: Crankcase, crankshaft, camshaft, piston(s), and connecting rod(s). Importation of these components together, whether assembled or unassembled, and whether or not accompanied by additional components such as a sump, carburetor spacer, cylinder head(s), valve train, or valve cover(s), constitutes an unfinished engine for purposes of these
Orders.
The inclusion of other products such as spark plugs fitted into the cylinder head or electrical devices (
e.g.,
ignition coils) for synchronizing with the engine to supply tension current does not remove the product from the scope. The inclusion of any other components not identified as comprising the unfinished engine subassembly in a third country does not remove the engine from the scope.
Specifically excluded from the scope of these
Orders
are “Commercial” or “Heavy Commercial” engines under 40 CFR 1054.107 and 40 CFR 1054.135 that have (1) a displacement of 160cc or greater, (2) a cast iron cylinder liner, (3) an automatic compression release, and (4) and a muffler with at least three chambers and volume greater than 400cc.
The engines subject to these
Orders
are predominantly classified in the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) at subheading 8407.90.1010. The engine subassemblies that are subject to these
Orders
enter under HTSUS 8409.91.9990. The mounted engines that are subject to these
Orders
enter under HTSUS 8433.11.0050, 8433.11.0060, and 8424.30.9000. Engines subject to these
Orders
may also enter under HTSUS 8407.90.1020, 8407.90.9040, and 8407.90.9060. The HTSUS subheadings are provided for convenience and customs purposes only, and the written description of the
Orders
is dispositive.
Continuation of the Orders

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) has conducted an administrative review of Navpad Pigments Private Limited (Navpad) regarding the countervailing duty order on carbazole violet pigment 23 (CVP-23) from India. The period of review (POR) is January 1, 2023, through December 31, 2023. In addition, Commerce is rescinding this review, in part, with respect to one company.
DATES:
Applicable October 26, 2026
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Dan Alexander, AD/CVD Operations, Office VII, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-4313
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On June 23, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the
Preliminary Results
of this administrative review and invited interested parties to comment.[1]
For a complete description of the events that occurred since the
Preliminary Results, see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.[2]
The Issues and Decision Memorandum is a public document and is on file electronically via Enforcement and Compliance's Antidumping and Countervailing Duty Centralized Electronic System (ACCESS). ACCESS is available to registered users at
https://access.trade.gov. In addition, the Issues and Decision Memorandum can be accessed directly at
https://access.trade.gov/frnotices.
Commerce conducted this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(B) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act).
Scope of the Order 3
The merchandise subject to the
Order
is carbazole violet pigment-23 from India. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
Rescission of Administrative Review, in Part
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), Commerce will rescind an administrative review, in whole or only with respect to a particular exporter or producer, if during the period covered by the review, there were no entries, exports, or sales of the subject merchandise, as the case may be. According to the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) import data on the record, the following company subject to this review did not have reviewable entries of subject merchandise during the POR for which liquidation is suspended: Sudarshan Chemical Industries Limited. Therefore, we are rescinding this administrative review with respect to this company, pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).[4]
Methodology
Commerce conducted this review in accordance with section 751(a)(1)(A) of the Act. For each of the subsidy programs found to be countervailable, we find that there is a subsidy,
i.e.
, a government-provided financial contribution that gives rise to a benefit to the recipient, and that the subsidy is specific.[5]
For a full description of the methodology underlying all of Commerce's conclusions,
see
the Issues and Decision Memorandum.
Analysis of Comments Received
All issues raised in the case and rebuttal briefs filed by parties in this review are listed in the appendix to this notice and addressed in the Issues and Decision Memorandum.

Preliminary Results, we made certain changes to the countervailable subsidy rate calculated for Navpad. For a discussion of these changes,
see

Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.212(b), Commerce shall determine, and CBP shall assess, countervailing duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of this review. For Navpad, Commerce will instruct CBP to assess countervailing duties at the subsidy rate listed in the table above. i.e., within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act. In accordance with section 751(a)(1) of the Act, Commerce intends to instruct CBP to collect cash deposits of estimated countervailing duties in the amount shown for the company listed above on shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the date of publication of the final results of this administrative review.
For all non-reviewed firms, we will instruct CBP to continue to collect cash deposits of estimated countervailing duties at the most recent company-specific rate applicable to the company or the all-others rate, as appropriate. Extension of Initiation of Investigations
The Petitions
On September 30, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) received antidumping duty (AD) and countervailing duty (CVD) petitions on imports of certain railway tank cars and parts thereof (tank cars) from Mexico filed in proper form on behalf of UTLX Manufacturing LLC (the petitioner), a domestic producer of tank cars.[1]
Determination of Industry Support for the Petitions
Sections 702(b)(1) and 732(b)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), require that a petition be filed by or on behalf of the domestic industry. To determine that the petition has been filed by or on behalf of the industry, sections 702(c)(4)(A) and 732(c)(4)(A) of the Act require that the domestic producers or workers who support the petition account for: (i) at least 25 percent of the total production of the domestic like product; and (ii) more than 50 percent of the production of the domestic like product produced by that portion of the industry expressing support for, or opposition to, the petition. Moreover, sections 702(c)(4)(D) and 732(c)(4)(D) of the Act provide that, if the petition does not establish support of domestic producers or workers accounting for more than 50 percent of the total production of the domestic like product, Commerce shall: (i) poll the industry or rely on other information in order to determine if there is support for the petition, as required by subparagraph (A); or (ii) if there is a large number of producers, determine industry support using a statistically valid sampling method to poll the industry.
Extension of Time
Sections 702(c)(1)(A) and 732(c)(1)(A) of the Act provide that within 20 days of the filing of an antidumping or countervailing duty petition, Commerce will determine,
inter alia,
whether the petition has been filed by or on behalf of the U.S. industry producing the domestic like product. Sections 702(c)(1)(B) and 732(c)(1)(B) of the Act provide that the deadline for the initiation determination, in exceptional circumstances, may be extended by 20 days in any case in which Commerce must “poll or otherwise determine support for the petition by the industry.” Because it is not clear from the Petitions whether the industry support criteria have been met, Commerce has determined it should extend the time period for determining whether to initiate the AD and CVD investigations in order to further examine the issue of industry support.
Commerce will need additional time to gather and analyze additional information regarding industry support. Therefore, it is necessary to extend the
( printed page 67289)
deadline for determining the adequacy of the Petitions by an additional 20 days. As a result, in accordance with sections 702(c)(1)(B) and 732(c)(1)(B) of the Act, Commerce's initiation determination will now be due no later than November 9, 2026.
International Trade Commission Notification
Commerce will contact the U.S. International Trade Commission (ITC) and will make this extension notice available to the ITC.

AGENCY:

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is simultaneously initiating and issuing the preliminary results of a changed circumstances review (CCR) of the antidumping duty (AD) order on heavy-walled rectangular welded carbon steel pipes and tubes (HWR) from Mexico, consistent with section 751(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), and 19 CFR 351.216 and 351.221(c)(3)(ii). Based on the information on the record, we preliminarily determine that Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V. (PLM) is the successor-in-interest to Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V. (PyH). Interested parties are invited to comment on these preliminary results.
DATES:
Applicable October 26, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Paola Aleman Ordaz, AD/CVD Operations, Office II, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: 202-482-4031.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On September 13, 2016, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the AD order on HWR from Mexico.[1]
On August 19, 2026, PLM informed Commerce that, effective July 11, 2017, it had changed its name from “Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V.” (
i.e.,
PyH) to “Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V.” (
i.e.,
PLM) and requested that Commerce conduct a CCR under 19 CFR 351.216(b) to determine that PLM is the successor in-interest to PyH for purposes of determining PLM's AD cash deposits and liabilities.[2]
On September 3, 2026, Commerce declined to initiate the CCR that PLM requested, citing the need for additional information pertaining to any changes in management, production facilities, customers, and suppliers.[3]
Therefore, Commerce issued a supplemental questionnaire to PLM, to which we received a timely response on September 21, 2026.[4]
We did not receive comments from other interested parties concerning this request.
Scope of the Order
The merchandise covered by the scope of the
Order
is HWR from Mexico. For a complete description of the scope of the
Order, see
the Preliminary Decision Memorandum.[5]
Initiation of Changed Circumstances Review
Pursuant to section 751(b)(1) of the Act, and 19 CFR 351.216, Commerce will conduct a CCR of an order upon receipt of information or a review request from an interested party for a review of an order which shows changed circumstances sufficient to warrant a review of the order.[6]
In the past, Commerce has used CCRs to address the applicability of cash deposit rates after there have been changes in the name or structure of a respondent, such as a merger or spinoff (“successor-in- interest,” or “successorship,” determinations).[7]
The information submitted by PLM supporting its claim that it is the successor-in-interest to PyH demonstrates changed circumstances sufficient to warrant such a review.[8]
The information submitted by PLM substantiates that its request is based solely on a change in the name of the company from “Perfiles y Herrajes LM, S.A. de C.V.” to “Perfiles LM, S.A. de C.V.” effective on July 11, 2017.[9]
Moreover, the evidence submitted in support of PLM's request demonstrates that PLM is otherwise the same business entity as PyH. Therefore, in accordance with the regulation referenced above, Commerce is initiating a CCR to determine whether PLM is the successor-in-interest to PyH.
Preliminary Results
Commerce is permitted by 19 CFR 351.221(c)(3)(ii) to combine the notice of initiation of a CCR and the preliminary results if Commerce concludes that expedited action is warranted. In this instance, because the record contains information necessary to make a preliminary finding, we find that expedited action is warranted and we have combined the notice of initiation and the preliminary results.
Accordingly, pursuant to section 751(b) of the Act, we have conducted a successor-in-interest analysis in response to PLM's request. In making a successor-in-interest determination in an AD CCR, Commerce examines several factors, including, but not limited to, changes in the following: (1) management and ownership; (2) production facilities; (3) supplier relationships; and (4) customer base.[10]
While no single factor or combination of factors will necessarily provide a dispositive indication of a successor-in-interest relationship, generally, Commerce will consider the new company to be the successor to the
( printed page 67290)
previous company if the new company's resulting operation is not materially dissimilar to that of its predecessor.[11]
Thus, if the evidence demonstrates that, with respect to the production and sales of the subject merchandise, the new company operates as essentially the same business entity as the former company, Commerce will assign to the new company the cash deposit rate of its predecessor.[12]
In its CCR request, PLM provided evidence demonstrating that PLM's operations are not materially dissimilar from those of PyH. Based on the record, we preliminarily determine that PLM is the successor-in-interest to PyH, as the change in the name was not accompanied by significant changes to its management and ownership, production, facilities, supplier relationships, or customer base. There is also no evidence of significant changes between PyH and the successor-in-interest company PLM's operations, ownership, or corporate or legal structure during the relevant period that could have impacted the successor-in-interest company's subsidy levels.[13]
Thus, we preliminarily determine that PLM operates as essentially the same business entity as PyH, that PLM is the successor-in- interest to PyH, and that PLM should receive the same AD cash deposit rate with respect to subject merchandise as its predecessor, PyH.
For a complete discussion of the information that PLM provided, and the complete successor-in-interest analysis,
see

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is rescinding the administrative review of the countervailing duty (CVD) order on common alloy aluminum sheet (CAAS) from the People's Republic of China (China), covering the period (POR) of January 1, 2025, through December 31, 2025.
DATES:
Applicable October 26, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Alexander Wolfe, AD/CVD Operations, Office VI, Enforcement and Compliance, International Trade Administration, U.S. Department of Commerce, 1401 Constitution Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20230; telephone: (202) 482-5826.
( printed page 67283)
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Background
On February 6, 2019, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
the CVD order on CAAS from China.[1]
On February 2, 2026, Commerce published in the
Federal Register
a notice of opportunity to request an administrative review of the
Order
.[2]
On March 31, 2026, pursuant to requests from interested parties,[3]
Commerce initiated an administrative review with respect to four companies: Alcha International Holdings Limited (Alcha International), Jiangsu Alcha Aluminum Co., Ltd. (Jiangsu Alcha), Yantai Jintai International Trade Co., Ltd. (Yantai Jintai), and Yinbang Clad Material Co., Ltd. (Yinbang).[4]
On April 6, 2026, we placed on the record U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) data for the entries of CAAS from China during the POR and invited interested parties to comment.[5]
No interested party submitted comments regarding the CBP data. The CBP data showed that Yantai Jintai and Yinbang were the only companies subject to this administrative review with suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR.[6]
On May 29, 2026, Yantai Jintai withdrew its request for an administrative review of itself.[7]
On June 29, 2026, the petitioner withdrew its request for an administrative review of Yinbang.[8]
No other interested party requested review of Yantai Jintai or Yinbang.
On June 30, 2026, Commerce notified interested parties that it intended to rescind the administrative review with respect to Alcha International and Jiangsu Alcha, because these companies did not have reviewable entries of subject merchandise during the POR for which liquidation is suspended.[9]
On August 3, 2026, Commerce issued a corrected notification of its intent to rescind the administrative review.[10]
No interested party submitted comments regarding Commerce's intent to rescind the administrative review.
Rescission of Review
Pursuant to 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3), it is Commerce's practice to rescind an administrative review of a CVD order where it concludes that there were no suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR for an exporter or producer.[11]
Normally, upon completion of an administrative review, the suspended entries are liquidated at the CVD assessment rate for the review period.[12]
Therefore, for an administrative review to be conducted, there must be a reviewable, suspended entry that Commerce can instruct CBP to liquidate at the calculated CVD assessment rate for the review period.[13]
As noted above, CBP entry data showed that there were no POR entries of subject merchandise for Alcha International or Jiangsu Alcha, the only companies for which requests for review were not withdrawn. Accordingly, in the absence of reviewable, suspended entries of subject merchandise during the POR, we are rescinding this administrative review, in its entirety, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.213(d)(3).
Cash Deposit Requirements
As Commerce has proceeded to a final rescission of this administrative review, no cash deposit rates will change. Accordingly, the current cash deposit requirements shall remain in effect until further notice.
Assessment Rates
Commerce will instruct CBP to assess countervailing duties on all appropriate entries. Countervailing duties shall be assessed at rates equal to the cash deposit of estimated countervailing duties required at the time of entry, or withdrawal from warehouse, for consumption, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.212(c)(1)(i). Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of this rescission notice in the
Federal Register
.
Notification Regarding Administrative Protective Order (APO)
This notice serves as a final reminder to parties subject to an APO of their responsibility concerning the return or destruction of proprietary information disclosed under APO in accordance with 19 CFR 351.305(a)(3), which continues to govern business proprietary information in this segment of the proceeding. Timely written notification of the return or destruction of the APO materials, or conversion to judicial protective order is hereby requested. Failure to comply with regulations and terms of an APO is a violation, which is subject to sanction.
Notification to Interested Parties
This notice is issued and published in accordance with sections 751(a)(1) and 777(i)(1) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended, and 19 CFR 351.213(d)(4).

Normally, Commerce will disclose to the parties in a proceeding the calculations performed in connection with the final results within five days of any public announcement or, if there is no public announcement, within five days of the date of publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.224(b). However, because Commerce made no changes to the
Preliminary Results
calculations, there are no new calculations to disclose.
Assessment Rates
Pursuant to section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act and 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1), Commerce has determined, and U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) shall assess, antidumping duties on all appropriate entries of subject merchandise in accordance with the final results of this review.
We calculated importer-specific
ad valorem
antidumping duty assessment rates on the basis of the ratio of the total amount of dumping calculated for the examined sales to the total entered value of those sales, in accordance with 19 CFR 351.212(b)(1). Where an importer-specific assessment rate is zero or
de minimis
(
i.e.,
less than 0.5 percent), we will instruct CBP to liquidate the appropriate entries without regard to antidumping duties. The final results of this administrative review shall be the basis for the assessment of antidumping duties on entries of merchandise covered by the final results of this review and for future deposits of estimated duties, where applicable.[7]
Commerce's “automatic assessment” practice will apply to entries of subject merchandise during the POR produced by TYCSA for which it did not know that the merchandise it sold to an intermediary (
e.g.,
a reseller, trading company, or exporter) was destined for the United States. In such instances, we will instruct CBP to liquidate unreviewed entries at the all-others rate established in the less-than-fair-value (LTFV) investigation (
i.e.,
14.75 percent),[8]
if there is no rate for the intermediate company(ies) involved in the transaction.[9]
Commerce intends to issue assessment instructions to CBP no earlier than 35 days after the date of publication of the final results of this review in the
Federal Register
. If a timely summons is filed at the U.S. Court of International Trade, the assessment instructions will direct CBP not to liquidate relevant entries until the time for parties to file a request for a statutory injunction has expired (
i.e.,
within 90 days of publication).
Cash Deposit Requirements
The following cash deposit requirements will be effective for all shipments of the subject merchandise entered, or withdrawn from warehouse, for consumption on or after the publication date of the final results of this administrative review, as provided by section 751(a)(2)(C) of the Act: (1) the cash deposit rate for TYCSA will be equal to the weighted-average dumping margin that is established in the final results of this review; (2) for previously investigated or reviewed companies not covered by this review, the cash deposit rate will continue to be the company-specific rate published for the most recently completed segment of this proceeding in which the company participated; (3) if the exporter is not a firm covered in this review, a prior review, or the LTFV investigation, but the producer is, the cash deposit rate will be the cash deposit rate established for the most recently completed segment for the producer of the subject merchandise; and (4) the cash deposit rate for all other producers or exporters will continue to be 14.75 percent, the all-others rate established in the LTFV investigation.[10]
These deposit requirements, when imposed, shall remain in effect until further notice.

On September 9, 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) received antidumping duty (AD) petitions concerning imports of certain corrugated die-cut cardboard boxes (corrugated die-cut boxes) [1]
from China, Malaysia, and Türkiye, filed in proper form on behalf of the American Pizza Boxes Manufacturers Coalition,[2]
and the United Steel, Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial and Service Workers International Union (the petitioners), the members of which are domestic producers of corrugated die-cut boxes and a certified union, which represents workers engaged in the production of corrugated die-cut boxes in the United States.[3]
The Petitions were accompanied by a countervailing duty (CVD) petition concerning imports of corrugated die-cut boxes from Türkiye.[4]
On September 29, 2026, Commerce extended the initiation deadline by 20 days to further examine the issue of industry support, because it was not clear from the Petitions whether the industry support criteria had been met.[5]
Between September 11 and October 9, 2026, Commerce requested supplemental information pertaining to certain aspects of the Petitions in supplemental questionnaires.[6]
Between September 15 and October 13, 2026, the petitioners filed timely responses to these requests for additional information.[7]
In accordance with section 732(b) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), the petitioners allege that imports of corrugated die-cut boxes from China, Malaysia, and Türkiye are being, or are likely to be, sold in the United States at less than fair value (LTFV) within the meaning of section 731 of the Act, and that imports of such products are materially injuring, or threatening material injury to, the corrugated die-cut boxes industry in the United States. Commerce also finds that the petitioners demonstrated sufficient industry support for the initiation of the requested LTFV investigations.[9]

SUMMARY:
In accordance with the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA), the Federal Trade Commission (FTC or Commission) is seeking public comment on its proposal to extend for an additional three years the Office of Management and Budget clearance for its Fuel Rating Rule (the Rule). The current clearance expires on October 31, 2026.
DATES:
Comments must be filed by November 25, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Interested parties may file a comment online or on paper, by following the instructions in the Request for Comment part of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section below. Written comments and recommendations for the proposed information collection should be sent within 30 days of publication of this notice to
www.reginfo.gov/public/do/PRAMain.
Find this particular information collection by selecting “Currently under 30-day Review—Open for Public Comments” or by using the search function. The
reginfo.gov
web link is a United States Government website produced by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the General Services Administration (GSA). Under PRA requirements, OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) reviews Federal information collections.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Hong Park, Attorney, Division of Enforcement, Bureau of Consumer Protection, Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20580, (202) 326-2158;
hpark@ftc.gov.
Type of Review:
Extension of a currently approved collection.
Likely Respondents:
(a)
Recordkeeping:
Refiners, Producers, Importers, Distributors, and Retailers of the Covered Fuel Types.
(b)
Disclosure:
Retailers of the Covered Fuel Types.
Estimated Annual Burden Hours:
28,163 (derived from 11,394 recordkeeping hours added to 16,769 disclosure hours).
Estimated Annual Labor Costs:
$455,731.
Estimated Annual Capital or Other Non-labor Costs:
$308,536.
Abstract:
The Fuel Rating Rule establishes standard procedures for determining, certifying, and disclosing the octane rating of automotive gasoline and the automotive fuel rating of alternative liquid automotive fuels, as required by the Petroleum Marketing Practices Act. 15 U.S.C. 2822(a)-(c). The Rule also requires refiners, producers, importers, distributors, and retailers to retain records showing how the ratings were determined, including delivery tickets or letters of certification.
Request for Comment
On July 23, 2026, the FTC sought public comment on the information collection requirements associated with the Rule. 91 FR 46439. Three commenters submitted germane responses. Two of the commenters supported the proposed extension of the OMB clearance for information collection requirements.[1]
A third commenter, The Native Claim Firm (“NCF”), expressed no position on the proposed extension but contested the Commission's burden estimate.[2]
Specifically, NCF observed that the Commission's burden estimate provides an average figure across retailers of all sizes and argued that this approach could obscure the relative burden on low-volume retailers. NCF requested the Commission to consider the burden on low-volume retailers and supplement its burden estimate with a breakdown by retailer size or dispenser count. To support its request, NCF estimated that low-volume retailers face a PRA burden of $0.0000077 per gallon, which is higher than the $0.0000057 per gallon that NCF calculated for the Commission's average figure approach. While the Commission appreciates commenters raising awareness that small entities may face unique compliance burdens, the Commission finds that this difference of two ten-thousandths of a cent per gallon does not warrant modifying the burden estimate in this instance.
Pursuant to the OMB regulations, 5 CFR part 1320, that implement the PRA, 44 U.S.C. 3501et seq.,
the FTC is providing this second opportunity for public comment while seeking OMB approval to renew the pre-existing clearance for the Rule. Your comment—including your name and your state—will be placed on the public record of this proceeding. Because your comment will be made public, you are solely responsible for making sure that your comment does not include any sensitive personal information, such as anyone's Social Security number; date of birth;
( printed page 67320)
driver's license number or other state identification number, or foreign country equivalent; passport number; financial account number; or credit or debit card number. You are also solely responsible for making sure that your comment does not include any sensitive health information, such as medical records or other individually identifiable health information. In addition, your comment should not include any “trade secret or any commercial or financial information which . . . is privileged or confidential”—as provided by Section 6(f) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. 46(f), and FTC Rule 4.10(a)(2), 16 CFR 4.10(a)(2)—including in particular competitively sensitive information such as costs, sales statistics, inventories, formulas, patterns, devices, manufacturing processes, or customer names.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Abstract
The High-Frequency Surveys Program was established as a natural progression from the creation of the Household Pulse Survey (HPS). The Census Bureau launched HPS in April 2020 as an experimental survey designed to rapidly collect and disseminate information on how emergent issues were affecting U.S. households from social and economic perspectives. HPS provided timely information during the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequently evolved to address other emergent social and economic issues facing households.
In 2024, HPS content began transitioning to a longitudinal design. In January 2025, HPS was incorporated into the Household Trends and Outlook Pulse Survey (HTOPS), which used a longitudinal design throughout 2025. Beginning in March 2026, HTOPS transitioned to an independent, cross-sectional design. The current cross-sectional design provides frequent opportunities to measure household trends and outlooks, understand changes in household conditions, and respond to emerging data needs while maintaining a flexible platform for experimentation and methodological research.
HTOPS is an experimental data product and an ongoing Census Bureau data collection platform designed to complement the Federal Statistical System's established statistical programs by deploying quickly and efficiently to measure household conditions and provide timely information on topics of social, economic, and demographic interest. The use of a stable, high-frequency platform allows the Census Bureau to respond to emerging issues, capture trends and outlooks, support related data needs, and conduct nationally representative field tests and methodological research in an efficient and reliable manner.
The HTOPS also supports research and development related to survey data collection and estimation. The platform can be used to conduct nationally representative field tests of questionnaire content, collection procedures, and other survey methods in support of Census Bureau and other Federal statistical programs. The Census Bureau may also investigate methods for enhancing survey data through administrative and other external data sources, developing modeled data products, and implementing adaptive design procedures that use auxiliary information. These activities can support improvements in data quality, operational efficiency, representativeness, and the usefulness of Federal statistics.
The HTOPS is primarily a Census Bureau data collection platform. Consistent with applicable law and subject to appropriate approvals and agreements, the platform may also support reimbursable surveys conducted under 13 U.S.C. 8(b). Such collections will use a Title 13 sampling frame and will be conducted subject to the applicable statutory, confidentiality, privacy, and statistical requirements.
The Census Bureau will document the methods used to collect, process, weight, and disseminate HTOPS data. Such documentation will provide information about the survey design and quality of resulting estimates, including response rates and weighting procedures, consistent with applicable Federal statistical standards and requirements.
II. Method of Collection
The Census Bureau will conduct the HTOPS electronically, using internally developed Business Enterprise systems as the data collection and management platform.
Invitations will primarily be sent by mail, and questionnaires will be administered primarily through internet self-response. Inbound computer-assisted telephone interviewing (CATI) will provide an additional response option for sampled households that do not wish to or cannot complete the questionnaire online. The Census Bureau may conduct outbound CATI nonresponse follow-up or automated reminder calls and may use SMS messages as a reminder or follow-up communication, as appropriate.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Abstract
The School District Review Program (SDRP) is sponsored by the U.S. Department of Education's National Center for Education Statistics (NCES) and is conducted annually by the U.S. Census Bureau (Census Bureau). It plays a critical role in determining each state's Title I allocation under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act, as amended by the Every Student Succeeds Act of 2015 (Pub. L. 114-95). School district data submitted through the SDRP combined with decennial census counts, Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates, and current population estimates inform the Census Bureau's estimates of children ages 5 to 17 living in poverty for each district. The U.S. Department of Education uses these estimates to distribute more than $18 billion in Title I funds each year.
The SDRP includes the review of Type 1, Type 2, and Type 3 school districts as defined by the NCES. Type 1 is a local school district that is not a component of a supervisory union. Type 2 is a local school district component of a supervisory union sharing a superintendent and administrative services with other local school districts. Type 3 is an education agency that performs administrative services for more than one school district, providing a common superintendent for participating districts.
SDRP participants include mapping coordinators and Title I Coordinators from all fifty states and the District of Columbia. Mapping coordinators, designated by state education agencies, review and update school district boundaries, names, grade ranges, levels, federal school district local education agency codes, and geographic relationships. Title I Coordinators oversee the program and review all materials.
II. Method of Collection
The SDRP consists of the Annotation Phase and Verification Phase. During the Annotation Phase, the Census Bureau provides mapping coordinators with its current school district boundary and attribute data. Mapping coordinators work with local school district, county, and state agency officials to review and update this information. Changes are submitted using the Geographic Update Partnership Software (GUPS), GUPS Web, and the digital submission log. The Census Bureau then reviews the submissions and updates the Master Address File/Topologically Integrated Geographic Encoding and Referencing (MAF/TIGER) System.
During the Verification Phase, the Census Bureau issues updated materials reflecting the processed changes. Mapping coordinators confirm whether updates were applied correctly and report any corrections, if necessary. New changes are not accepted during the Verification Phase.
Annual Schedule
The Annotation Phase occurs every year in December/January.
The Annotation Phase submission deadline occurs every year in March.
The Verification Phase occurs every year in May, with a one-week review period.

SUMMARY:
This action establishes Class E airspace at Graham Hospital Heliport, Canton, IL. This action supports new instrument procedures and instrument flight rule (IFR) operations.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority for This Rulemaking
The FAA's authority to issue rules regarding aviation safety is found in Title 49 of the United States Code. Subtitle I, Section 106 describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII, Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the agency's authority. This rulemaking is promulgated under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart I, Section 40103. Under that section, the FAA is charged with prescribing regulations to assign the use of airspace necessary to ensure the safety of aircraft and the efficient use of airspace. This regulation is within the scope of that authority as it establishes Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface at Graham Hospital Heliport, Canton, IL, to support IFR operations.
History
The FAA published an NPRM for Docket No. FAA-2026-9505 in the
Federal Register
(91 FR 51602; August 11, 2026) proposing to establish Class E airspace at Graham Hospital Heliport, Canton, IL. Interested parties were invited to participate in this rulemaking effort by submitting written comments on the proposal to the FAA. One comment expressed support for the NPRM. The commentor also requested that the FAA design the instrument approach corridors as compactly as safety allows to minimize lateral airspace expansion and preserve local VFR transit routes.
Class E5 airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface already existed in the Canton, IL, area prior to this rule to protect instrument procedures for Peoria International Airport (PIA). The current action (26-AGL-18) does not alter or expand the existing Class E airspace footprint over the City of Canton or impact VFR flight corridors in the Canton area.
Incorporation by Reference
Class E airspace designations are published in paragraph 6005 of FAA Order JO 7400.11, Airspace Designations and Reporting Points, which is incorporated by reference in 14 CFR 71.1 on an annual basis. This document amends the current version of that order, FAA Order JO 7400.11M, dated July 30, 2026, and effective September 15, 2026. These amendments will be published in the next update to FAA Order JO 7400.11. FAA Order JO 7400.11M, which lists Class A, B, C, D, and E airspace areas, air traffic service routes, and reporting points, is publicly available as listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this document.
The Rule
This action modifies 14 CFR part 71 by establishing Class E airspace extending upward from 700 feet above the surface within a 6.3-mile radius of Graham Hospital Heliport, Canton, IL. This action is the result of instrument procedures being developed for this heliport to support IFR operations.
Regulatory Notices and Analyses
The FAA has determined that this regulation only involves an established body of technical regulations for which frequent and routine amendments are necessary to keep them operationally current. It, therefore: (1) is not a “significant regulatory action” under Executive Order 12866; (2) is not a “significant rule” under DOT Order 2100.6B, “Rulemaking and Guidance Procedure” (March 10, 2025); and (3) is expected to result in, at most, de minimis costs from compliance with applicable operating requirements or minor flight rerouting for operators choosing to navigate around the controlled airspace. Since these amendments are routine and the expected impact to operators is de minimis, the FAA certifies that this rule, when promulgated, does not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities under the criteria of the Regulatory Flexibility Act.
Environmental Review
The FAA has determined that this action qualifies for categorical exclusion under the National Environmental Policy Act in accordance with FAA Order 1050.1G, “FAA National Environmental Policy Act Implementing Procedures,” paragraph B-2.5(a), which categorically excludes from further environmental impact review rulemaking actions that designate or modify classes of airspace areas, airways, routes, and reporting points

The FAA also determined that no extraordinary circumstances exist that warrant preparation of an environmental assessment or environmental impact statement.

articles.full_text: In this document, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) exempts video programmers for public, educational, and governmental access (PEG) channels from the requirement to register with the Commission and to certify captioning compliance if the PEG video programmers provide video programming exclusively to PEG channels that are exempt from closed captioning requirements. Additionally, providers of PEG programming are relieved of filing obligations if the administrators of non-exempt PEG channels certify compliance for programming carried on such channels. The Commission similarly exempts providers of programming carried on nonbroadcast networks for distribution by a cable operator or other multichannel video programming distributor (MVPD) from certifying when the nonbroadcast network itself certifies that it is exempt or that all programming comprising the network's linear line-up is either exempt from or compliant with the closed captioning rules.

articles.full_text:
Here’s the first part of my theory: cybercriminals are not the organized geniuses we implicitly imagine. Anyone building a criminal gang has to find candidates willing to forgo more stable opportunities in the formal economy. My modeling estimated that something like 720,000 people are involved in the online criminal economy, 90% of them in scam and fraud call-center type operations, some of them human-trafficked. Of the 76k or so actual hackers, the vast majority work for governments. Of the remaining few thousand criminal hackers, most work in ransomware. Some demographic estimates of these workforces are below.
Criminal organizations need to base themselves in middle and lower income countries, where they can pay less and hire people who have few formal-economy options. For scams and fraud, picture an illegal call center building in a small city in Nigeria. For ransomware gangs, picture kids working in the informal economy in Belarus. I think folks in the AI safety and cyber world sometimes imagine adversaries as their Waluigi twins, implicit MIT graduates; in fact, in cybercrime we’re dealing with a lower-skill demographic. articles.full_text:
Here is the audio, video, and transcript.  Here is one excerpt:

Cowen: Talk me out of this worry: So we agree science is an ecosystem, and there’s always a temptation to want to fund the most dynamic, most productive parts of the ecosystem. And right now, that would probably be A.I.
But if you need the whole ecosystem to be working well, arguably you should be funding, at the margin, the less productive parts, which need the aid. That will sometimes be universities, but there’s plenty of other inefficient parts of our ecosystem.
So is this plan not putting more resources into the parts that are working well, but we get stuck with bottlenecks if the parts that are not working well end up with fewer resources?
Kratsios: Well, luckily, we’re not investing all of our money for the federal government into S.I. for science. It’s a portfolio approach. And obviously one ——
Cowen: But it’s a net shift toward artificial intelligence, right?
Kratsios: Well, I would argue — and I think this is a very important distinction — it’s not investing in superintelligence, it’s investing in superintelligence for science.
So the question is, I think a lot of people argue: Oh, why would the federal government want to invest more in superintelligence when billions, if not trillions, of dollars are being invested in the private sector into superintelligence? And I would agree with that statement. We shouldn’t be doing that.
The government isn’t funding how to create a next frontier model. That’s something that our great American companies are working on.
But applying those models to scientific discovery is still in its early stages. And as you know, if you think about the trend or the path by which we’ve gotten to this place with L.L.M.s — we started first with being able, essentially, to scrape the whole corpus of the internet, to use that to train a large language model.
The next chapter of that was around coding, where the model builders realized: Oh, we have really good coding data, and we can actually train these models to be good at coding. So then we had this rise of Anthropic and OpenAI Codex and all this stuff.
And I think, to me, the next chapter is around science, and the data that you need to train these large language models for science is still one that we’re working on a lot. And we were very proud to announce 190 federal data sets being made public in order to help train these science models.
But ultimately, you’re going to be applying this superintelligence to everything from material science to chemistry to math to physics, and we have to be in a position to actually leverage that.

Pursuant to the provisions of Section 19(b)(1) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Act”) [1]

The Commission is publishing this notice to solicit comments on the proposed rule change from interested persons.
I. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Terms of Substance of the Proposed Rule Change
The Exchange proposes to amend the fee schedule (the “Fee Schedule”) applicable to MIAX Pearl Equities, an equities trading facility of the Exchange, to make a non-substantive, clarifying change to add liquidity indicator codes “Ep” and “Fp” below the table titled “Midpoint Peg Order Adding Liquidity at Midpoint Volume Tiers” in Section 1)e) as those liquidity indicator codes have been applicable since they were first established.
II. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
In its filing with the Commission, MIAX Pearl included statements concerning the purpose of and basis for the proposed rule change and discussed any comments it received on the proposed rule change. The text of these statements may be examined at the places specified in Item IV below. MIAX Pearl has prepared summaries, set forth in sections A, B, and C below, of the most significant aspects of such statements.
( printed page 67376)
A. Self-Regulatory Organization's Statement of the Purpose of, and Statutory Basis for, the Proposed Rule Change
1. Purpose
The Exchange proposes to amend Section 1)e) of the Fee Schedule to make a non-substantive, clarifying change to add liquidity indicator codes “Ep” and “Fp” below the table titled “Midpoint Peg Order Adding Liquidity at Midpoint Volume Tiers” as those liquidity indicator codes have been applicable to such executions since they were first established.
The Exchange currently provides a standard rebate of ($0.00200) [3]
per share for executions of Midpoint Peg Orders [4]
in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO [5]
and add liquidity to the Exchange in all Tapes.[6]
The Exchange also provides enhanced rebates through a tiered pricing structure for executions of Midpoint Peg Orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO and add liquidity to the Exchange in all Tapes based on an Equity Member [7]
achieving certain “Midpoint ADAV” thresholds (defined below) (the “Midpoint Volume Tiers Program”).[8]
Pursuant to the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program, Midpoint ADAV means the average daily added volume (“ADAV”) for the current month consisting of Midpoint Peg Orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO and add liquidity to the Exchange.[9]
Pursuant to Tier 1 of the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program, Equity Members may qualify for an enhanced rebate of ($0.0025) per share for executions of Midpoint Peg Orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO and add liquidity to the Exchange by achieving a Midpoint ADAV equal to or greater than 500,000 shares. Pursuant to Tier 2 of the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program, Equity Members may qualify for an enhanced rebate of ($0.0027) per share for executions of Midpoint Peg Orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO and add liquidity to the Exchange by achieving a Midpoint ADAV equal to or greater than 1,000,000 shares. Pursuant to Tier 3 of the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program, Equity Members may qualify for an enhanced rebate of ($0.0029) per share for executions of Midpoint Peg Orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO and add liquidity to the Exchange by achieving a Midpoint ADAV equal to or greater than 1,500,000 shares.
In February 2025, the Exchange filed a proposed change [10]
to, among other things, establish liquidity indicator codes and associated fees and rebates for orders executed during the Early Trading Session and Late Trading Session.[11]
In that filing, the Exchange established certain liquidity indicator codes applicable to executions of Midpoint Peg Orders in securities priced at or above $1.00 per share that execute at the midpoint of the Protected NBBO and add liquidity to the Exchange in all Tapes during the Early Trading Session and Late Trading Session (liquidity indicator codes “Ep” and “Fp,” respectively).[12]
At that time, liquidity indicator codes “Ep” and “Fp” should have been included as applicable codes in the sentence below the table in Section 1)e) of the Fee Schedule pertaining to the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program.
The Exchange now proposes to amend the sentence below the table in Section 1)e) of the Fee Schedule to add liquidity indicator codes “Ep” and “Fp” as those codes have been applicable to the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program since they were established in February 2025. The Exchange notes that the rebates provided by the Midpoint Volume Tiers Program have been correctly applied to Equity Members' trading activity since the Early Trading Session and Late Trading Session were introduced, including since the time the Exchange established liquidity indicator codes “Ep” and “Fp.” The Exchange does not propose to amend any rebates or fees. The purpose of the proposed change is to provide greater clarity within the Fee Schedule.

On May 5, 2026, the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA or Government) issued an Order to Show Cause (OSC) to Vida Janson, M.D., of Seattle, Washington (Respondent). OSC, at 1, 3. The OSC proposed the revocation of Respondent's DEA Certificate of Registration No. BJ6418380, alleging that Respondent is “without authority to prescribe, administer, dispense, or otherwise handle controlled substances in the State of Washington, the state in which [she is] registered with DEA.”
Id.
at 2 (citing 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3)).
On June 3, 2026, Respondent filed a request for a hearing and filed a Supplemental Answer to the allegations in the OSC. Respondent also filed a Motion to Hold Proceeding in Abeyance seeking to defer the proceeding until
( printed page 67332)
resolution of the underlying state authority matter. On August 7, 2026, the Government filed a Motion for Summary Disposition, which Respondent opposed. On August 27, 2026, Chief Administrative Law Judge Derek C. Julius (Chief ALJ) granted the Government's Motion for Summary Disposition and recommended the revocation of Respondent's registration, finding that because Respondent lacks state authority to handle controlled substances in Washington, the state in which she is registered with DEA, “there is no other fact of consequence for this tribunal to decide in order to determine whether or not she is entitled to maintain her DEA registration.” Order Granting the Government's Motion for Summary Disposition, and Recommended Rulings, Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, and Decision of the Administrative Law Judge (RD), at 5. Respondent did not file exceptions to the RD.
Having reviewed the entire record, the Agency adopts and hereby incorporates by reference the entirety of the ALJ's rulings, findings of fact, conclusions of law, and recommended sanction as found in the RD and summarizes and expands upon portions thereof herein.
Findings of Fact
Effective January 23, 2026, the Washington State Department of Health issued a Findings of Fact, Conclusions of Law, and Final Order suspending Respondent from the practice of medicine in the State of Washington as a result of Respondent committing unprofessional conduct. OSC, at 2.[1]
According to Washington online records, of which the Agency takes official notice, Respondent's Washington medical license is suspended.[2]
Washington State Department of Health Provider Credential Search,
https://wahelms.my.site.com/s/license-search
(last visited date of signature of this Order). Accordingly, the Agency finds that Respondent does not have the state authority to handle controlled substances in Washington, the state in which she is registered with DEA.[3]
Discussion
Pursuant to 21 U.S.C. 824(a)(3), the Attorney General is authorized to suspend or revoke a registration issued under section 823 of the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) “upon a finding that the registrant . . . has had his State license or registration suspended . . . [or] revoked . . . by competent State authority and is no longer authorized by State law to engage in the . . . dispensing of controlled substances.” With respect to a practitioner, DEA has also long held that the possession of authority to dispense controlled substances under the laws of the state in which a practitioner engages in professional practice is a fundamental condition for obtaining and maintaining a practitioner's registration.
Gonzales
v.
Oregon,
546 U.S. 243, 270 (2006) (“The Attorney General can register a physician to dispense controlled substances `if the applicant is authorized to dispense . . . controlled substances under the laws of the State in which he practices.' . . . The very definition of a `practitioner' eligible to prescribe includes physicians `licensed, registered, or otherwise permitted, by the United States or the jurisdiction in which he practices' to dispense controlled substances. § 802(21).”). The Agency has applied these principles consistently.
See, e.g.,James L. Hooper, M.D., 76 FR 71371, 71372 (2011), pet. for rev. denied, 481 F. App'x 826 (4th Cir. 2012); Frederick Marsh Blanton, M.D., 43 FR 27616, 27617 (1978); Scott Hansen, A.P.R.N.,90 FR 27338 (2025).[4]
According to Washington statute, “[a] practitioner may dispense or deliver a controlled substance to or for an individual or animal only for medical treatment or authorized research in the ordinary course of that practitioner's profession.” Wash. Rev. Code § 69.50.308(j) (2025). Further, a “prescription” means “an order for controlled substances issued by a practitioner duly authorized by law or rule in the state of Washington to prescribe controlled substances within the scope of his or her professional practice for a legitimate medical purpose.”
Id.
at § 69.50.101(41). Finally, a “practitioner” as defined by Washington statute includes “[a] physician licensed to practice medicine and surgery.”
Id.
at § 69.50.101(40)(c).
Here, the undisputed evidence in the record is that Registrant currently lacks authority to practice medicine in Washington. As already discussed, an individual must be a licensed practitioner to dispense or prescribe a controlled substance in Washington. Thus, because Registrant lacks authority to practice medicine in Washington and, therefore, is not authorized to handle controlled substances in Washington, Registrant is not eligible to maintain a DEA registration in Washington. RD, at 7. Accordingly, the Agency will order that Registrant's DEA registration be revoked.
Order
Pursuant to 28 CFR 0.100(b) and the authority vested in me by 21 U.S.C. 824(a), I hereby revoke DEA Certificate of Registration No. BJ6418380 issued to Vida Janson, M.D. Further, pursuant to 28 CFR 0.100(b) and the authority vested in me by 21 U.S.C. 823(g)(1), I hereby deny any pending applications of Vida Janson, M.D., to renew or modify these registrations, as well as any other pending application of Vida Janson, M.D., for additional registration in Washington. This Order is effective November 25, 2026.

Cost-of-Living Increases
General
The cost-of-living increase is 3.6 percent for monthly benefits under title II and for monthly payments under title XVI of the Act. Under title II, OASDI monthly benefits will increase by 3.6 percent for individuals eligible for December 2026 benefits, payable in January 2027 and thereafter. We base this increase on the authority contained in section 215(i) of the Act.
Pursuant to section 1617 of the Act, Federal SSI benefit rates will also increase by 3.6 percent effective for payments made for January 2027 but paid on December 31, 2026.

Computation of the cost-of-living increase is based on an increase in a Consumer Price Index (CPI) produced by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. At the time the Act was amended to provide automatic cost-of-living increases starting in 1975, only one CPI existed, namely the index now referred to as CPI for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). Although the Bureau of Labor Statistics has since developed other CPIs, we follow precedent by continuing to use the CPI-W. We refer to this index in the following paragraphs as the CPI.
Section 215(i)(1)(B) of the Act defines a “computation quarter” to be a third calendar quarter in which the average CPI exceeded the average CPI in the previous computation quarter. ACTION:
Notice of availability.
SUMMARY:
This notice advises the public that two direct take permits 1454-3R and 1455-3R have been issued for operation, monitoring, and evaluation of a hatchery program rearing and releasing sockeye salmon in the Snake River basin of Idaho, and that the decision documents are available upon request.
DATES:
Permits 1454-3R and 1455-3R were issued on October 7, 2026, subject to certain conditions set forth therein. The permits expire on September 27, 2036.
ADDRESSES:
Requests for copies of the decision documents or any of the associated documents should be directed to the West Coast Region NMFS Office, 1201 NE Lloyd Blvd., Portland, OR 97232.
Sockeye salmon (Oncorhynchus nerka): endangered, naturally and artificially propagated Snake River Sockeye Evolutionary Significant Unit (ESU);
Chinook salmon (O. tshawytscha): threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Snake River Spring/Summer-run ESU; threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Lower Columbia River Chinook salmon ESU;
Steelhead (O. mykiss): threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Snake River Steelhead Distinct Population Segment (DPS); threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Lower Columbia River Steelhead DPS; threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Middle Columbia River Steelhead DPS; threatened, naturally and artificially propagated Upper Columbia River Steelhead DPS.
Background
The operators and funding agencies, including Idaho Fish and Game, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribe, Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife, NMFS's Northwest Fisheries Science Center, the Nez Perce Tribe and Bonneville Power Association, submitted a Hatchery and Genetic Management Plan to NMFS pursuant to NMFS' ESA section 10(a)(1)(A) for hatchery activities in the Snake River basin.
The programs are intended to contribute to the survival and recovery of Snake River Sockeye salmon in the Snake River basin. The proposed program would maintain the Snake River sockeye salmon captive broodstock, collect and spawn adult
( printed page 67302)
sockeye salmon returning to the Snake River basin, rear juveniles, and release eggs, juveniles, and adult fish in upper Salmon River basin lakes, as well as into Tanner Creek, Oregon. Adult fish that return to Tanner Creek, would be transported to Eagle Fish Hatchery, Idaho for processing, and released to spawn upstream in Redfish and Pettit Lake. The proposed continuation of the program would indicate best management practices to minimize adverse effects on the ESU.

AGENCY:
Federal Bureau of Investigation, Department of Justice.
                    SUMMARY:
The purpose of this notice is to announce a meeting of the Federal Bureau of Investigation's (FBI) Criminal Justice Information Services (CJIS) Advisory Policy Board (APB). The CJIS APB is a federal advisory committee established pursuant to the Federal Advisory Committee Act (FACA). This meeting announcement is being published as required by Section 10 of the FACA.
                    DATES:
The APB will meet in open session from 8:30 a.m. until 5:00 p.m. on December 09-10, 2026.
                    ADDRESSES:
The meeting will take place at the Omni Oklahoma City Hotel, 100 Oklahoma City Blvd., Oklahoma City, OK 73109; telephone: 405-438-6500. The CJIS Division is offering a blended participation option that allows individuals to participate in person or to participate via a telephone bridge line. The public will be permitted to provide comments and/or questions related to matters of the APB prior to the meeting. Please see details in the supplemental information.
            
                SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The FBI CJIS APB is responsible for reviewing policy issues and appropriate technical and operational issues related to the programs administered by the FBI's CJIS Division, and thereafter, making appropriate recommendations to the FBI Director. The programs administered by the CJIS Division are the Law Enforcement Enterprise Portal, National Crime Information Center, Next Generation Identification, National Instant Criminal Background Check System, National Data Exchange System, and Uniform Crime Reporting.
The meeting will be conducted with a blended participation option. The public may participate as follows: via phone bridge number to participate in a listen-only mode or in person. Participants attending in person are required to check-in at the meeting registration desk.
                    Registrations may be submitted via email to 
                    agmu@leo.gov.
                     Information regarding the phone access will be provided prior to the meeting to all registered individuals. Interested persons whose registrations have been accepted may be permitted to participate in the discussions at the discretion of the meeting chairman and with approval of the Designated Federal Officer (DFO).
                
Any member of the public may file a written statement with the APB. Written comments shall be focused on the APB's issues under discussion and may not be repetitive of previously submitted written statements. Written comments should be provided to Mr. Nicky J. Megna, DFO, at least seven (7) days in advance of the meeting so the comments may be made available to the APB members for their consideration prior to the meeting.
Individuals requiring special accommodations should contact Mr. Megna by no later than December 02, 2026. Personal registration information will be made publicly available through the minutes for the meeting published on the FACA website.
                    Nicky J. Megna,
CJIS Designated Federal Officer, Criminal Justice Information Services Division, Federal Bureau of Investigation.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), 5 U.S.C. 552, and the Privacy Act of 1974 (PA), 5 U.S.C. 552a, provide individuals the right to request access to federal agency records, subject to certain exemptions and exclusions. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) regulations at 6 CFR part 5 implement these statutes for DHS components, including U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
ICE Form I-902, Freedom of Information Act Request Form, is used to collect the minimum information necessary for ICE to:
Identify the subject of the requested records;
Locate, retrieve, and review potentially responsive records;
Verify the identity of the requester and, when applicable, confirm the requester's authority to receive records about another individual; and
Process requests under FOIA and/or the Privacy Act in accordance with statutory and regulatory requirements.
This collection is necessary for ICE to fulfill its statutory obligations to process FOIA and Privacy Act requests, document requesters' identities and consents, and maintain accurate records of requests and disclosures. Failure to collect this information would impede ICE's ability to comply with FOIA and the Privacy Act, and with DHS FOIA implementing regulations.
Indicate How, by Whom, and for What Purpose the Information Is To Be Used
The information collected on ICE Form I-902 is used by:
ICE FOIA Office personnel;
FOIA and Privacy Act staff within relevant ICE program offices (e.g., Enforcement and Removal Operations and Homeland Security Investigations (HSI); and
Other DHS or federal personnel as needed for coordination and consultation.
The information is used to:
Positively identify the subject of the records and the requester;
Determine the scope and type of records being requested (e.g., ERO apprehension/detention records, SEVP records, other ICE records);
Locate and retrieve responsive records in ICE systems and files;
Verify consent and authority to access records relating to a third party (Part 3);
Satisfy identity verification requirements under FOIA/PA and DHS regulations (Part 4—declaration under penalty of perjury or notarized affidavit);
Document the request in ICE's FOIA case tracking systems for processing, quality control, and reporting; and
Support required FOIA program reporting and audit activities.
This is a new collection specific to ICE Form I-902. Previously, similar information has been collected through freeform written FOIA/PA requests submitted via mail or other electronic means. The form standardizes and structures the necessary data elements to improve completeness, accuracy, and processing efficiency.
ICE Form I-902 is made available to requesters in electronic format (fillable PDF) via the ICE public website. Requesters may complete the form electronically, print, and submit it via the methods permitted by ICE FOIA (
e.g., upload through the online FOIA portal or mail), consistent with current ICE FOIA procedures.
The information from the completed form is entered into, or ingested by, ICE's FOIA case tracking and document management systems (
e.g., SharePoint-based matter tracking systems and other FOIA case management tools) as described in DHS/ALL-001 and DHS/ALL-004 and associated Privacy Impact Assessments. ICE uses these systems to:
Log and track FOIA/PA requests;
Assign requests for processing;
Record processing milestones and determinations; and
Maintain an electronic record of correspondence and responsive documents.

The form is designed to:
Be fillable electronically to reduce handwriting errors and incomplete submissions;
Align data elements with FOIA tracking system fields to minimize rekeying and reduce data entry burden; and
Facilitate electronic storage, retrieval, and reporting.
ICE has considered and implemented the use of information technology to the extent practicable to re-duce burden on both requesters and the government, consistent with FOIA requirements for multiple submission channels (mail, electronic, etc.) and the need for original signatures for identity verification.
This collection primarily affects individuals who are requesting access to records about themselves or another individual. In limited circumstances, small businesses or other small entities (such as law firms or non-profit organizations) may submit requests on behalf of clients or as organizational requesters.
The burden on such entities is minimal because:
The form is short, straightforward, and limited to information necessary to identify the re-quester/subject and locate records;
The form is available in a fillable PDF format that can be reused as a template by organizations that regularly submit requests; and
Only one form is required per request, and no specialized equipment or software is needed beyond standard office tools.
