We are soliciting public comments to permit the Department to:
Evaluate whether the proposed information collection is necessary for the proper functions of the Department.
Evaluate the accuracy of our estimate of the time and cost burden for this proposed collection, including the validity of the methodology and assumptions used.
Enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected.
Minimize the reporting burden on those who are to respond, including the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology.
Please note that comments submitted in response to this Notice are public record. Before including any detailed personal information, you should be aware that your comments as submitted, including your personal information, will be available for public review.
Abstract of Proposed Collection
This information collection relates to three final rules published on January 27, 2026. 91 FR 3319, 91 FR 3332, and 91 FR 3345. These rules implement the President's Protecting Human Flourishing in Foreign Assistance (PHFFA) policy, by requiring recipients of U.S. foreign assistance funds to agree to certain terms and conditions. In summary, foreign NGOs, U.S. NGOs, and international organizations are required to comply with the policy (foreign governments and parastatals may also be required to comply with the policies, but those entities are not “persons” under the Paperwork Reduction Act, thus not covered by this notice) and agree that during the period of the award they will segregate records so that the Department can verify that they are not violating the terms of the foreign assistance grants that were provided to them. Full details are included in the three final rules.
Methodology
There is no form involved in this information collection. The final rules require recipients of U.S. foreign assistance funds to maintain records and make business records available upon request, which is a requirement governed by the Paperwork Reduction Act. In accordance with 2 CFR 200.334, all recipients need to preserve records. The final rules require U.S. NGOs to ensure that any program, project, or activity for which funds are made available under a Department award must be organized so that the program, project, or activity is physically and financially separate from any “prohibited activities” undertaken using other funding sources. Foreign assistance grantees must ensure that all award terms flow down to any subrecipients of such assistance, as applicable.

InterAction's central argument is that the Department's burden estimates fail to capture the real operational costs of PHFFA compliance, particularly because the regulations require organizations to assess activities and funding streams beyond a single U.

Government award.
Training costs are understated: one member organization consolidated training across three related regulations but still had to run both introductory and specialized HR-focused sessions, with more anticipated as interpretation evolves—meaning these are recurring, not one-time, costs.
A second major cost driver is ambiguity around allowable activities; without clear definitions or standardized documentation expectations, organizations cannot direct compliance resources efficiently and must repeatedly engage legal review.

donors to assess overall organizational compliance, and in some cases provide technical assistance to partners struggling to interpret the rules against their own funding structures.

InterAction's asks are narrow and specific: clarify the scope of monitoring for non-federally-funded activities, and ensure any new compliance IT tools integrate with existing nonprofit systems rather than adding parallel administrative layers.

articles.full_text: In this document, the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) modifies rules to ensure that consumers can revoke consent for robocalls they no longer wish to receive while continuing to receive those they still want. We also modernize our rules to ensure that consumers have clear, simple, and automated ways to revoke consent while streamlining callers' ability to process revocations. Specifically, we allow callers to interpret a revocation request as applying only to the specific category of informational robocalls to which the revocation was directed, allow callers to designate an exclusive means to revoke consent, and amend the exemption from the consent requirement for financial institutions to allow them to more easily alert customers to fraudulent activity on their account. In addition, we delegate authority to the Consumer and Governmental Affairs Bureau (CGB) in consultation with the Enforcement Bureau (EB) to review our robocall rules to ensure that those rules are clear and easy to read.

The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is amending its regulations to facilitate direct leveraging of prior U.S. Department of Energy or Department of War authorizations of demonstration reactors into the NRC's licensing reviews of commercial reactor facility applications that reference those designs. This rulemaking improves NRC licensing review efficiency, where applicable, by explicitly establishing by regulation an additional means for reactor applicants to demonstrate the safety functions of their reactor designs, thereby contributing to the safe and secure use and deployment of civilian nuclear energy technologies.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on November 25, 2026.

On May 23, 2025, President Donald J. Trump signed Executive Order (E.O.) 14300, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.” Section 5, “Reforming and Modernizing the NRC's Regulations,” directed the NRC to undertake a review and wholesale revision of its regulations and guidance documents as guided by the policies set forth in section 2 of the E.O. This rulemaking addresses section 5(d), which contemplates an expedited pathway to approve reactor designs that the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) or the Department of War (DOW) have tested and that have demonstrated the ability to function safely.[1] E.O. 14300 further states that NRC review of such designs should focus solely on risks that may arise from new applications permitted by NRC licensure, rather than revisiting risks that have already been addressed in the DOE or DOW processes.
II. Discussion
Consistent with its authority and historical practice under section 161 of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (AEA) to make, promulgate, issue, rescind, and amend rules and regulations as well as that under section 182 of the AEA to determine the information that enables the Commission to make the findings required to grant an application for a utilization facility, the NRC is amending title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) section 50.43, “Additional standards and provisions affecting class 103 licenses and certifications for commercial power,” and section 53.440, “Design requirements.” These changes explicitly establish a pathway for streamlined reviews for licensing commercial reactor designs that have previously received

DOE or DOW authorization and that have been tested and have demonstrated the ability to function safely. The amendment to § 50.43 explicitly establishes such a pathway for the licensing frameworks under 10 CFR part 50, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” and part 52, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,” and the amendment to § 53.440 does so for the 10 CFR part 53, “Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Commercial Nuclear Plants,” licensing framework. A similar provision is included in a separate proposed rule, “Licensing Requirements for Microreactors and Other Reactors With Comparable Risk Profiles,” which, if finalized, would apply to the associated proposed 10 CFR part 57, “Licensing Requirements for Microreactors and Other Reactors with Comparable Risk Profiles,” licensing framework (91 FR 23628; May 1, 2026). The primary intent of this rulemaking is to improve NRC licensing review efficiency, and in turn increase capacity, for conducting licensing reviews. At the same time, this rulemaking maintains flexibility for the NRC to leverage a broad range of technologies, testing methods, and information from previously authorized and evaluated designs, as appropriate and supported by an applicant in its commercial license application. In turn, this contributes to the safe and secure use and deployment of civilian nuclear energy technologies.
Section 50.43(e) provides two options for license applicants to demonstrate how newer reactor designs, including those that use simplified, inherent, passive, or other innovative means, accomplish their safety functions. AGENCY:
Department of Commerce (Department).
ACTION:
Final rule; correcting amendment.
SUMMARY:
By this action, the Department makes a correcting amendment to its regulations governing testimony by its current and former employees and the production of its documents in legal proceedings. The Department previously amended those regulations via final rule by removing and/or replacing language that is redundant, that references other authorities, or that provides only unnecessary elaboration. One of the amendatory instructions set forth in that rule, however, indicated that certain introductory text and a certain subparagraph were being amended when, in fact, no such amendments were made to those portions. This action merely corrects that inaccurate amendatory instruction and does not make any further changes to the regulations.
DATES:
The rule is effective October 26, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Daniel Sweeney, Deputy General Counsel for Economic, Statistical, and Regulatory Affairs, Office of the General Counsel, at (240) 474-3619.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On October 19, 2026, the Department issues a final rule amending 15 CFR part 15 by removing and/or replacing language that is redundant, that references other authorities, or that provides only unnecessary elaboration (91 FR 65964). In that final rule, amendatory instruction 5 indicated, among other things, that the Department was amending the introductory text for § 15.14(g) as well as the contents of § 15.14(g)(2). However, the final rule did not make any such amendment for either. This action corrects that inaccurate amendatory instruction and does not make any further changes to part 15.
Regulatory Classifications
A. Administrative Procedure Act
Pursuant to 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the Department finds good cause to waive the prior notice and opportunity for public participation requirements of the Administrative Procedure Act for this action. The Department considers this action to be uncontroversial, and has determined that prior notice and opportunity for public participation is unnecessary, because this action only corrects an inaccurate amendatory instruction; this correction will ensure that the amendatory instructions properly reflect the amendments made by the rule. For the same reason, the Department has determined that delaying the effectiveness of this corrective action would be contrary to the public interest; this action will correct an omission and remove a potential source of confusion without introducing any new cost for the public. The Department therefore finds good cause to waive the public notice and comment period under 553(b)(B) and to waive the 30-day delay in effectiveness under 553(d).
B. Executive Orders 12866, 14192, and 13132
This rule is not significant pursuant to Executive Order (E.O.) 12866. This rule is an E.O. 14192 deregulatory action. This rule does not contain policies having federalism implications as the term is defined in E.O. 13132.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
Because a notice of proposed rulemaking and an opportunity for public participation are not required to be given for this rule by 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B), the analytical requirements of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 601et seq.) are not applicable. Accordingly, no regulatory flexibility analysis is required, and none has been prepared.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
